body: {"total":6,"records":[{"title":"Direct-to-CT transfer on the ambulance stretcher and door-to-needle times at a regional stroke centre: an improvement report","authors":"Oduya-Hartmann L, Pike-Mensah R, Solberg-Achebe T","year":2019,"venue":"Stroke Pathway Improvement","doi":"10.5555/spi.2019.0052","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"At a regional stroke centre treating about 100 patients a year with thrombolysis, direct transfer to CT on the ambulance stretcher and pre-notification reduced median door-to-needle time from 58 to 36 minutes over 18 months. The proportion treated within 45 minutes rose from 31 to 69 percent. Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 5 percent of treated patients before and 4 percent after the change. Treatment of stroke mimics rose from 2 to 5 percent. Night and weekend cases improved less than weekday daytime cases, and the authors describe the out-of-hours pathway as the next target."},{"title":"Process mapping of acute stroke thrombolysis pathways: where do the minutes go?","authors":"Castellanos-Nyberg A, Obi-Fairweather K, Haddad-Lund M","year":2022,"venue":"Journal of Acute Neurology Services","doi":"10.5555/jans.2022.0138","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In four hospitals, observers timed 160 thrombolysis cases step by step. The largest delays occurred between arrival and CT (median 17 minutes) and between CT and the treatment decision (median 14 minutes). Drug preparation added a median of 7 minutes when it started after the decision. Delays were longest when the stroke physician was not present at arrival. Hospitals that paged the whole team with one call had shorter arrival-to-CT times than hospitals that called team members one by one."},{"title":"Door-to-needle times at night and weekends: an analysis of a regional stroke dataset","authors":"Lindqvist-Adeyemi P, Brennan-Tanaka S","year":2017,"venue":"Regional Stroke Services Review","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using a regional stroke dataset of 3,420 thrombolysis cases, median door-to-needle time was 12 minutes longer at night and at weekends than in weekday daytime. The difference was largest in hospitals where the stroke registrar was on call from home. Out-of-hours patients were not more severely affected on arrival. Hospitals that had moved to a single group page for the stroke team showed a smaller out-of-hours gap. The analysis could not separate the effect of staffing from the availability of imaging and radiographers, which also fell out of hours in most hospitals."},{"title":"Balancing measures in stroke thrombolysis improvement: haemorrhage and stroke mimics","authors":"Achterberg-Silva J, Nakamura-Oyelaran D","year":2024,"venue":"Stroke Pathway Improvement","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed 22 improvement reports that shortened door-to-needle times. Twelve reported symptomatic haemorrhage and nine reported treatment of stroke mimics. Symptomatic haemorrhage did not rise in any report, while treated mimics rose in four reports, reaching 6 percent in one. Most reports had too few patients to detect a change in haemorrhage. We recommend reporting both measures with their numerators and denominators, not only rates, and reviewing every treated mimic. Reports that reviewed every treated mimic described most as migraine, seizure or functional presentations with a benign course."},{"title":"Statistical process control with small monthly samples: run charts for door-to-needle times","authors":"Varga-Okonkwo H, Reid-Castellano B, Sato-Lindgren E","year":2020,"venue":"Quality Measurement in Health Care","doi":"10.5555/qmhc.2020.0091","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Stroke centres treating fewer than ten patients a month produce unstable monthly medians. Using simulation and data from 30 hospitals, we show that case-by-case run charts of individual door-to-needle times, with a median line and the standard run rules, detect a sustained 15-minute improvement within about 20 cases, whereas monthly medians need five to six months. An individuals chart can flag unusually long cases for review without waiting for a monthly summary. The authors provide a template and advise freezing the baseline median before any change is tested."},{"title":"Team debriefs after every thrombolysis case: feasibility and time to treatment","authors":"Ferreira-Mwangi O, Holt-Nakashima R","year":2025,"venue":"Journal of Acute Neurology Services","doi":"10.5555/jans.2025.0024","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In two hospitals, the treating team held a two-minute debrief after each thrombolysis case, recording the main delay on a card. Debriefs were held after 81 percent of cases. Staff described them as blame-free when a nurse led them. Median door-to-needle time fell by 9 minutes over six months, alongside other changes. Recorded delays most often concerned CT availability and paging. Night teams held debriefs less often than day teams. The authors could not separate the effect of debriefs from the other changes made at the same time."}]}
